newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanese Christians announce opposition front.
newsitem.headline: Lebanese Christians announce opposition front.

text.p: Three prominent Lebanese Christian leaders opposed to Syria's dominant role in Lebanon announced on Thursday the formation of an opposition front to work to regain what they called their country's lost sovereignty.

The birth of the "National Gathering" front was announced in Beirut by Dori Chamoun, head of the National Liberal Party, who said it also groups supporters of rebel General Michel Aoun and former president Amin Gemayel. Aoun and Gemayel live in Paris.

The three rightwing Maronite leaders, who fiercely oppose the presence of Syria's 35,000 troops in Lebanon and often attack Lebanese rulers as Syrian puppets, urged other Lebanese opposition forces to join the front.

"The National Gathering's founders call on all Lebanese, resident and expatriate, to mull the current circumstances our dear homeland is passing through and the grave dangers facing all of us," Chamoun told a news conference.

"Sovereignty is breached, dignity missing, democracy deformed, the parliamentary system inoperative, freedoms chained, human rights usurped and reconciliation cancelled," added Chamoun, who often meets Aoun and Gemayel in Paris.
The announcement came a day before Lebanon celebrates the 53rd anniversary of its independence from France.

Aoun, who has waged an abortive 1989 "War of Liberation" to oust Syrian troops from Lebanon, has not returned to Lebanon despite the lapse of his five-year exile term this summer. He was ousted in a Syrian-led blitz in 1990.
The three Maronite leaders had called on Lebanese to boycott recent parliamentary elections in which pro-Syrian Christian and Moslem candidates won an overwhelming victory.

But the Lebanon-based Christian opposition ignored the call, dividing the Christian minority over whether to vote and losing badly in the polls. The month-long vote was also marred by accusations of fraud.
Many Christians say their community emerged weakened from the 1975-90 civil war and that Christian members of the half-Moslem half-Christian government do not truly represent them.

Shaker Aoun, Gemayel's representative at the news conference, said relations between Lebanon and Syria should be "consolidated on the basis of acknowledging the independence and the sovereignty of each of the two states."
He called for the formation of a national unity government that "would prepare for free and honest polls" in Lebanon.
Chamoun said the Taif peace accord -- which ended the civil war in 1990 by giving Moslems equal political power -- was being implemented by the government in a "selective way".
One of the pact's articles calling for the return of the hundreds of thousands of Lebanese displaced by the war -- many of them Christians -- was not fully implemented, Chamoun said.
"Pertaining to this tragic situation Lebanese have only two choices: resign from the homeland...or confront democratically ...to stop the collapse and save the homeland," he added.
